utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. Before we start with the first witness, the Chamber would like to raise three matters. The first one relates to the last hearing of last week. At the end of our last hearing on the 2nd of June, 2010, we dealt with two exhibits the Prosecution moved for leave to amend its 65 ter exhibit list with them. As we were already over time that day, the Chamber did not rule on that motion. The Defence didn't object to this motion. Now leave is granted. The documents P312 and P313 [sic], marked for identification, should be added to the 65 ter exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In addition to that, it has come to the Chamber's attention, in contrast to the material submitted with its Rule 92 ter motion, the Prosecution now wishes to tender Witness PW-025's original witness statements provided to the OTP as his Rule 92 ter statement instead of his testimony in the Popovic case which was submitted to the Chamber in connection with the Rule 92 ter motion. The Chamber notes that its decision on the 92 ter motion, which provisionally admitted both, first the Popovic transcripts and, secondly, those exhibits which had been admitted through PW-025 in the Popovic case, was based on an analysis of the transcript of the Popovic testimony as the Rule 92 ter statement in this case, not the underlying witness statement provided to the OTP. The Chamber thus considers that the Prosecution seeks what amounts to a variation of the Chamber's Rule 92 ter decision of the 3rd of November, 2009. The Chamber considered it's potentially problematic that the Prosecution is seeking such a variation in a relatively informal and last-minute fashion. In the future, such requests should be made in a timely written filing in order to allow time for the Chamber to consider the effect of such a substitution on its previous analysis of the evidence proposed for admission in the Rule 92 ter motion and for the accused to have adequate time to prepare for cross-examination. With regard to the evidence of PW-025, however, the Chamber is mindful of the benefits of admitting a more concise witness statement for which there already exists a B/C/S translation, despite the lack of notice to the Chamber and the accused. Moreover, in light of the fact that Mr. Tolimir has been on notice of the fact that the Prosecution would be seeking the admission of the witness statement, albeit as an accompanying exhibit rather than as a Rule 92 ter statement itself, since the filing of the motion in February 2009, it would appear that there would be no prejudice to the Defence if the Chamber were to permit such a substitution in the instant case. Mr. Tolimir, do you have any objections to raise in this regard?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will take your word for it. If you believe there will be no problems, then I will take that for granted. Currently, I am unable to recall all of the arguments we put forth in our submissions when discussing this particular topic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Accordingly, once the witness attests that the underlying witness statement reflects what he would say if examined, the Chamber will admit it pursuant to Rule 92 ter, along with the 11 intercepts named therein, which it considers inseparable and indispensable from the underlying statement. The third point I would like to mention is the very urgent -- extremely urgent confidential motion we received yesterday from Mr. Tolimir. Mr. Thayer, would you like to comment on that? Do you have anything to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, General Tolimir, my learned friends. Good morning, everyone. We are in receipt of the proposal. I don't know whether it's the Trial Chamber's preference to have written submissions or oral submissions. I'm available now to address the issue in a shorter or slightly longer fashion, depending on the Court's wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would appreciate if you could deal with this problem of this motion now, orally, because we have the witnesses scheduled for today and tomorrow, so that it is -- an urgent decision is needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I'll move, then, as quickly as I can, Mr. President. Having had an opportunity last night to review the proposal, I frankly see nothing presented there, either in fact or in law, which would necessitate or warrant this pretty radical proposal to just put the brakes on the intercept operators completely. I should say at the outset that the Prosecution, of course, has absolutely no objection should the Defence desire/intend to adduce expert testimony on any issue, particularly in connection with the intercepts, as we're dealing with them now. Frankly, we had expected to see these kinds of motions pre-trial or earlier. We had been encouraging the Defence to do so. We've been trying to persuade the Defence to put its case, as I think you've heard us on a number of occasions, to the witnesses so that we can really clarify what the issues are that are to be joined in this trial, particularly when we have these almost 20 intercept operators who are about to come in. I think one thing that this urgent proposal raises, one issue it brings up, is precisely how important it is for the Defence now to be up-front with the Chamber and with the Prosecution about what its theory is, what its case is, with respect to these intercepts. And that is important for a number of reasons. The primary two reasons, I think, are: One, fairness to the witnesses themselves when they come here to testify under Rule 90 -- I think it's 90(G). I'll check, but it's somewhere in Rule 90 where a party is expected to put its case to the witness. And if it is the Defence's case in this case that these intercepts are fraudulent, they're manufactured after the event, with the necessary implication/accusation that these witnesses were part of that or, in fact, a continuing part of that, since they're coming here to testify about their contemporaneous notations and transcriptions of these intercepts, then under Rule 90 and under any fair trial rights concept of which I am aware, that should be put to the witnesses so that there is no doubt about what the Defence's case is. On the other hand, if the Defence's case is that it accepts this process, generally speaking, that this interception was going on, that these note-books were used at the time, but that at some point after the war portions were inserted in between entries, then that should be presented to the witnesses so that the witnesses understand what they are being essentially accused of, so we can join the issues, and so that they can be framed in a clear manner and not lying in wait for further down the road, in which case we may be forced to bring these witnesses back if they're not properly confronted with these issues. So from -- secondly, from a trial efficiency perspective, I believe it's very important that this issue be raised now, that we have an idea what the general's case is with respect to these intercepts. On the third hand, if his position is, I accept the authenticity of these intercepts, at least in certain circumstances, and we do see occasions when General Tolimir appears to accept the authenticity of the intercepts when it suits him; for example, in his pre-trial brief he relies heavily on a number of intercepted conversations that he believes are in his favour, then we need to know that, too. And from our perspective, he can have it all three ways, if he wants. There's no and/or here or one or the other. He can have it all three ways, but we need to know what his case is going to be. And, again, we have no problem with expert testimony in this issue. I think, and I'll have to consult with Mr. McCloskey, but I don't see a problem, for example, if he can get it together quickly enough, that we would have that testimony come in in the Prosecution's case in chief. In that way, we could have the full scope of this testimony at an earlier stage, and the Trial Chamber would be perhaps in a position to deal with it sooner than later and have this intercept issue resolved, which may benefit, again, the clarity and efficiency of the trial. As for the mechanics of any expert testimony, we have to liaise with the Defence to make the proper arrangements. We need to know who the expert is, what kind of tests we're talking about, what kind of experts we're talking about. The accused is in the same position as any other party in terms of expert testimony. We need to know and have proper notice of what that's going to be. And in terms of maintaining the proper chain of custody and the physical integrity of the evidence itself, in this case the note-books, we need to liaise to some degree on that before we can, I think, take the next steps, if the Defence is serious about presenting expert testimony on this issue. And what we've seen so far, I think, is a -- and I don't mean this ini a necessarily pejorative way, but we've seen, I think, a certain coyness on behalf, rightly speaking, of the Defence with respect to its case. You may recall in -- during the testimony of the witness who just completed his testimony, there was some questioning by the accused on this issue of the date on the note-book and so forth, but the actual theory, the challenge to the witness that this witness was part of manufacturing/fabricating these note-books, was not put directly to the witness. And particularly when we have witnesses coming in here who were sitting down -- they will testify about sitting down, having their headphones on, recording the conversations, transcribing them themselves in these note-books, working with the cryptography, being involved in the whole process, it's particularly important for that case to be put to those witnesses if for no other reason for out of fairness to the witnesses. I think one of the most important issues that I saw in the proposal is why the -- why the sudden urgent need to shut down the testimony. Why now, when everybody has known from the beginning of this trial, in its pre-trial stages, that this testimony was coming? There is no surprise at all about this testimony. The accused cannot credibly claim that he was surprised in any way by any of this testimony or the disclosure that he refers to in his filing. He knows -- the Defence knows that these issues were raised in the examination of Prosecution witnesses in the last case; he knows that they were raised specifically in the Defence's pre-trial brief or briefs in the Popovic case; counsel for Beara cross-examined witnesses on these issues; the Beara and Vujadin Popovic team both raised these issues in their final briefs; and, again, the accused, himself, again, depending on whether it suits him or not with respect to how he views the authenticity of these intercepts, the accused himself raised this issue in his response to our 92 bis proposal almost a year ago. And, again, he was being coy in the response. If you read the response, he said, I'm not going to tell you what my theory is because I don't want the Prosecution to be able to tailor its examination and give away my cross, but I've got -- basically, he says, I've got issues with the authenticity of these note-books. So he's known for a long time that this was going to be part of his case. So why we have the urgency now all of a sudden is not present in the proposal, and I don't think there is a legitimate reason that this has to be -- that this needs to stop these proceedings. The accused can put the proposition of his case, whatever the -- whatever his theory is, he can put that proposition, without having his expert report in his hand, to any intercept operator that comes. We can assume -- let's just assume, for the sake of argument, that his expert report concludes, yes, that there was multiple handwriting or that these note-books were manufactured after the war. He can put those propositions to these witnesses without having to wait and delay the trial proceedings. He's already done that, as I said, in a coy way. He questioned the last witness on that very issue. So I see no reason to suspend these intercept operators from testifying. We've got them here, and, in fact, the first three intercept operators are MUP intercept operators who didn't even use note-books. So that's just not even an issue on the table for these witnesses. I think I'll stop there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Thayer. Mr. Tolimir, do you want to comment on this and add something to your written motion of yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Greetings to all those present. A prayer follows. I wanted to say the following: When the Prosecutor was speaking about the submission I filed, stated that I put forth my own Defence thesis; however, I'm not doing that. I only want the truth to surface here. I examined a witness for a whole day who was the boss of all these operators who collected intercepts. In his presence, while examining him, I asked him whether these reports could be treated in real time. He said they were able to do so in spite of the fact that even the most up-to-date services were unable to do that. He said he needed only two hours to do so, whereas the most modern services and equipment requires at least four. I also asked him whether they exchanged data. He said they did not. Thirdly, we found the note-book, which speaks for itself. We shouldn't discuss any Tolimir's thesis here, but we should only consider what is the truth. We have already asked for an expert, which needs to be approved by the Registry. This expert will do his own part, and Tolimir wishes for nothing but the truth. If the Prosecutor has the same intention as I do for the truth to surface, then they shouldn't oppose anything that would go against that. I see no reason for that. We should all know the truth. The Prosecutor is not to be blamed for any untruths presented here. Secondly, I didn't want to accuse anyone. I'm not the Prosecutor here. I am the accused. I can only put questions to witnesses. I cannot accuse them of anything. I can only ask them whether they did something or did not. I wasn't coy at all. I spent days analysing the reports of those services who created intercepts before we even had an armed force. This should not become personal. Everything I do is aimed at discovering the truth. I filed my submission in such a fashion because I believe the expert we are requesting could be -- could deal with this rather quickly. This is his profession, and it is only up to the Registry when this person would be allowed to do so and when he would be able to receive the material in question. Nothing is up to Tolimir. I'm not trying to obstruct anything. I accept anything this Court decides, irrespective of whether this contributes to the truth or not. I am trying to make the truth known, but the ultimate decision is yours. This is all I wanted to say for now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Before your decision, I wanted to state another fact. The Prosecutor stated that I accept certain things when they are in my favour, whereas I don't accept them in other situations. It is not up to me to accept or not any reports. I never invoked any particular reports of these witnesses or any intercepts that can be found in the note-book. Please do bear in mind I even allowed them to include those elements pertaining to me. I don't want the truth not to be made known for something having been omitted previously. I want everything out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber, after having considered all arguments, finds itself in a quite complicated situation. The Chamber is of the opinion that we have to make clear that the rights of the accused have to be preserved. We must guarantee a fair trial, but, on the other hand, also an expeditious trial. The motion received yesterday in the late afternoon comes at a very late stage of this procedure. Nevertheless, the parties and the Chamber was able to consider the reasoning of the motion and took into account nothing about the truth. If these documents are real -- if these note-books are real documents produced at the time or not, this is to be decided at the end of the trial. The Chamber is of the opinion that the accused has every possibility to challenge the evidence, as Mr. Tolimir did with the first two witnesses, intercept supervisors, during cross-examination. The accused has every possibility to call witnesses, including expert witnesses, in the Defence case, and if there is any reason, after having received the expert report of the expert witness about these note-books, then it might be the case that the witnesses we have heard about the note-books should be recalled, if there is a reason at that stage of the trial. And as the Prosecution offered, it will do its very best to assist an expert witness with the material to be checked. And in the end, the Chamber is of the view that there is no limitation -- no violation of the rights of the accused if the Chamber is continuing the hearings with intercept witnesses. But to make it very clear, it is up to the Chamber, at the end of this trial, after having heard witnesses and after having received evidence, if these note-books can be accepted as evidence or not. The Chamber gives weight to all evidence, including documents, at the end of the whole case. To summarise that, the Chamber is of the view that the stay of the hearings, which would result in the cancellation of several days of hearings, is not the proper way to deal with this motion. The Chamber will deny -- is now denying this motion but especially will preserve the rights of the accused to have a fair trial. This is very clear. After this decision, the Chamber is prepared to start with the next witness, and the witness should be brought in. I think there are -- just a moment. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I apologise. It seems that you're rejecting my proposal. Does it mean that you are also rejecting my proposal for the engagement of an expert in these proceedings? I proposed that with a good intention. I proposed that other witnesses be heard before the expert provides his opinion about the testimony of those witnesses. Please bear that in mind. I could not send my request sooner because only yesterday I received materials from the Prosecutor that formed the base for the submission of my motion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Tolimir, the Chamber's decision was very clear. It was only dealing with your request not to hear the intercept witnesses today and the following days of our hearings and to have, in fact, a cancellation of hearing days. This motion is denied. We were not dealing at all with your request for -- to have an expert witness about the origin of these note-books. We are not dealing with that problem at the moment today. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, while the witness is being brought in, I have two quick housekeeping matters, just to keep the Court informed. We have two --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: While the witness is being brought in the screens should be closed because he must have the possibility to come in and to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes. We have two English translations -- here we go. We have two English translations for P00159 and P00160, and they are now up-loaded in the e-court. We understand that the Chamber wishes to be advised when these are made available, so they are there now. And they were previously MFI'd, so now they're received in the English translation and they're up-loaded. With respect to the Chamber's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could we perhaps deal with that first?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: These two exhibits will be exhibits and no longer marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. With respect to the Chamber's second issue today with respect to the Prosecution's informal and last-minute fashion, for which I take full responsibility - that was my informality and last-minuteness - there are two subsequent witnesses for whom, as the Trial Chamber noted, we are doing the same thing. Does the Trial Chamber wish written filings with respect to those two witnesses, or do I have a pass for those two witnesses? We're certainly -- we'll certainly file a written notice if that's what the Court wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, please be patient for a moment, and the screens should be opened. Dealing with your last question, the Chamber dealt with these three witnesses already. That was our decision. But in future that should be made clear in a more formal way. That would assist the Chamber and the accused in the preparation of the evidence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. And I take the opportunity to mention that this morning the first matter I raised, there was a mistake. I was not dealing with -- in fact, with the document P313, but P314. I was just told that there was a mistake. Now, sir, excuse me that we dealt with some procedural matters. You are welcomed to the Tribunal. Would you now please read allowed the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. You know that there are protective measures in place for you so that you will not be addressed with your full name, and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- your voice and your face will not be known outside this courtroom. Please, the parties should switch off the microphones while the witness is answering questions. Mr. Thayer, do you have examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I do. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 6288, that is, P305, up in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Witness, you'll see a document appearing on your screen shortly. When you were here last, this document was handed to you in hard copy, but now we're going to look at the computer for it. I just ask you to confirm whether you see your name on this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution would tender P305.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The witness said he sees it. Could the witness state that this is his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is my name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This will be received under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall providing a signed witness statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in January of 2007?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Yes, I recall having provided that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Witness, did you read that signed witness statement in your own language when we met I think it was a week ago yesterday?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Yes, I did read the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Witness, can you attest before this Trial Chamber that that witness statement accurately reflects what you said during your interview with the Office of the Prosecutor in January of 2007?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Yes, this is the statement that I provided in 2007, which I signed, and which I subsequently read a few days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just so the record is clear, Witness, can you attest that that statement is a fair and accurate representation of what you told the OTP in January of 2007?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Witness, during that interview, were you shown a booklet or packet of 11 intercepts?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, again, when we met last Monday, did you again review those 11 intercepts in connection with your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And were you able to determine whether or not you personally took part in intercepting, recording, transcribing, and transmitting those intercepts, those conversations?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Yes, I did take part in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And with the assistance of Madam Usher, I'm going to hand you an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I just ask you to look at the first 11 tabs in that booklet. On the side, there are 11 tabs. I ask you to kindly leaf through those 11 tabs and tell the Trial Chamber whether or not you can confirm again that you took part in intercepting these 11 conversations.

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Yes, I've reviewed the 11 reports and can confirm that they are my reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I know it's been a week since you saw them, sir, but can you confirm whether or not those are the 11 intercepts you were shown during your interview in 2007?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Yes, they were shown to me. They are the ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Witness, finally, with respect to your 2007 witness statement, can you attest before this Trial Chamber that if you were asked the same questions today that you were asked back then, during your interview, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would tender the witness's witness statement under seal - that's P292 - as well as the 11 intercepts which have been identified by the Registry by P number 293 to 303. Just to save a little bit of time, I did not show him the actual witness statement, but he did confirm that he had reviewed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: First I would like to clarify one date. This is P299. In your list or in the Registry's list - I'm not sure about that - it is stated the 22nd of July, 1995, 2335 hours, but, in fact, this is a document of the 23rd of July, with the same time. And the witness referred to it in the statement also as a document on number 0320-1509 to -- 0320-1509 of the 23rd of July, 1995. Just to be very clear which document you are referring about.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm just taking a look at it right now. I think I see where that notation came from, and it's -- maybe we can just ask one question of the witness and clarify that for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If you would turn to tab 7 of your booklet, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we can look at P299. Again, this is under seal, so it shouldn't be broadcast, but on e-court it's 299.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Witness, just so we know we're looking at the same document, do you see an eight-digit number in the upper right-hand corner of this intercept report?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you see --

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Yes, I can see the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And does it end in 1508, 1508?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: When we look at report number 832, if you can locate that one at the bottom of the page, do you see an intercept with the time of 2335 hours?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what is the date of this particular report number 832?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: The 23rd July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we look above at report number 831, which is the report immediately preceding report number 832, do you see an intercept, a report, of 2305 hours?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what is the date of that report that's listed there, sir?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: 22nd July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you have any idea or explanation or can you tell the Court whether the dates on these two reports appeared to you to be correct or not? And if you can't draw any conclusions, that's fine, too. We're just asking for your help. We have one document here with two dates and two times which are fairly close together, so we're just asking for some clarification. If you can supply that for the Trial Chamber, please.

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: To be honest, at this moment I can't tell you exactly what happened. This report here was late, and the typing and sending could have spilled over to the next day, which did happen if a report was received late in the evening. I really can't remember what happened in this particular case. It may be an error as well. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's look at the next intercept in your packet, which is at tab 8 of your booklet. We just looked at reports 531 and 532.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, for e-court purposes, this is P300, and it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, we just looked at reports number 831 and 832. Do you see report 833 on your screen or in your booklet, sir? Again, this is P300.

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it, yes. I can see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what is the time on this intercept?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: 00.35, 23rd of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, again, having seen the subsequent report coming out shortly after midnight, and I note for the record that this intercept is dated, as you said, 23 July 1995, report number 833, does that help you at all in explaining to the Trial Chamber whether you can determine whether the date on report number 832, the one that precedes this, is correct or not?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: It is possible that there was a mistake in the date or, rather, in the time. There may have been a mistake in the way the time was recorded. Or just bear with me for a moment, please. Or perhaps a mistake was made in recording the date. The reports always followed each other in sequence, unless a report arrived very late and was typed late, and then it was sent the following day, whereby the correct date was recorded on the report with the time indicated, the time from the previous day.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, unless there are any further inquiries from the Chamber, I think we'll leave it there and move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. The documents P292 to P303 will be received under seal, and the document -- the pseudonym sheet will be P305, under seal. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will have a few extra questions for this witness, but first I'd like to read the summary of the witness interview. And I think we can remain in public session for the entirety of the summary. The witness was interested in radio since elementary school because his brother was involved in a local Ham Radio club, then became active in Ham Radio clubs himself as a teenager and received his B Category Ham Radio license in 1998 -- that's -- pardon, 1988. He began working for the MUP in 1990 in the communications section of a public security sector. From 1992 to 1995, the witness worked in the MUP as a signalsman, typing, encrypting, and transmitting documents to other MUP stations. In June of 1995, he was temporarily assigned to the State Security Sector, which was short two men, so he and a colleague were loaned to that unit at the northern site, where he worked as an intercept operator for more than six months. The witness described the procedure used when intercepting, taping, and transcribing VRS radio communications as follows: He would monitor the channels on frequencies which they had selected. When he began recording a conversation, he would note the date, time, channel, and frequency on a piece of paper. Afterwards, he would transcribe the conversation onto paper. If any portion was inaudible, he would indicate it with three dots. The most important aspect was to achieve 100 per cent accuracy. They would listen to conversations many times, if necessary, and sometimes several of them would listen to the same conversation. Sometimes the typist would be asked to listen to the tape with headphones on to assist in an accurate transcript. Sometimes the operator and the typist would both listen to a tape on a speaker. Sometimes the witness would dictate intercepts he had taped directly to the typist. They did not always transcribe the entire conversation which they had typed -- I beg your pardon, which they had taped, if portions of it were unimportant, that is, if passages were not of any military interest. If the information was urgent, they would sometimes transcribe directly from the tape into the computer. The witness and his colleague worked as a team and helped each other in all aspects of intercepting and transmitting these conversations, performing all aspects of the job. Most of the time, the witness worked as the intercept operator and his colleague worked as the typist because his colleague was a faster typist and the witness had more radio experience, but they took turn doing these tasks. The witness reviewed 11 intercept print-outs and recognised them as his and confirmed that he intercepted and recorded them. And that ends the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Witness, I just wanted to follow up on a couple of areas to expand on your statement a little bit and your prior testimony. You said in your witness statement and during the last trial that you and your colleague worked together, very closely, intercepting these conversations. Can you describe for the Trial Chamber, please, what types of tasks you would work together closely doing? Just if you could give the Trial Chamber a brief flavour of how you actually worked together as a team.

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Would you like me to illustrate that with an example of our team-work?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sure, I think that would be helpful. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Well, I can give you this example: If I was seated by the radio set, listening in on a conversation, and for the most part the conversations we intercepted at that time were urgent in nature, in such cases, the colleague who was next to me would come close. We had UHER recorders, and we would use them to record those conversations. Then together we would listen to the conversation in question again, and he usually noted it down since he had better handwriting. If the conversation was urgent, he would type it directly into the computer. If some things were unclear, we would listen to particular portions over and over. And, if necessary, we would even ask the assistance of another colleague in order to confirm what they could hear if we were uncertain of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could we please pause for a moment. There is a technical problem with the earphones. Perhaps we should continue talking. Was it again the problem of the B/C/S language? Witness, could you please repeat the last two or three sentences.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's no problem. In such a case when I intercepted a conversation, we would listen to it again from the UHER recorder --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. I cannot hear the witness, whereas I can hear you well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could anybody work on that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps you can put the question to the witness, and with his answer we will see if the problem is solved.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, would you please tell the Trial Chamber just a little bit about how the shift system worked for you and your colleagues at the northern site?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: At the outset, the shifts took two to three days when we just arrived in June. However, at some later stage, we began taking turns every seven days. There would be our team, that is to say, me and my colleague, who would stay there for seven days, and then another team would come in. And the same system applied until the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Are we doing okay, Mr. President? All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No complaint by Mr. Tolimir, so we should carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Carry on, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's take a look again at your booklet that you have in front of you, sir. And I'd ask you to take a look at now tabs 12 through 23 of your booklet. And I just want to first ask you: Do you recall me showing you an additional dozen intercepts when we met last Monday?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if you'd kindly flip through those 12 intercepts from tabs 12 to 23, and I would ask you whether you can tell the Trial Chamber, once you've had a chance to refresh yourself, whether or not you participated in intercepting, recording, transcribing, or transmitting those intercepts.

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Yes, I did participate in either interception, recording, or transcription of these conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how can you tell? How are you able to make that determination, sir?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: First and foremost, I can tell that by the time of the conversations as well as the topics discussed and participants included. I can also tell by my signature which follows each and every intercept, be it as the first or the second name. In any case, my name always appeared following the intercepts. I can also say that I still recall many of those conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I note for the record that tabs 12 through 22 run from 8 July through 10 July of 1995 and that the last intercept is dated 25 July. With respect to the intercepts between 8 and 10 July, tabs 12 through 22 - and we're speaking about P306 to 316 just for the record - you just testified that you recall some of these actual intercepts. Can you clarify a little bit -- provide a little bit more detail for the Trial Chamber how it is that you're able to recall anything about any of these intercepts?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Certainly I recall them, especially those which included certain high-ranking UN officials such as Generals Janvier and Nicolai and perhaps Mr. Gobillard. I recall them because at the time it was my great wish that those conversations would amount to something. I still carry that feeling within me. This is how I can recall certain details from those conversations. They are still with me. Of course, there are such conversations which I remember to a lesser extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. President, at this time I would tender Exhibits P306 to P316. And if we could just take a look at ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to clarify the time and the number again. If you look at P316, dated 10th of July, 1995, I don't find it in the binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We'll see if we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you help us?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'll see if I can help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Because tab 22 contains an intercept of the 10th of July, 1995, at 2015 hours. That might be the previous month. It may be a misinterpretation on my side, but perhaps you can clarify this.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. President. What we should be looking at - and perhaps we can call it up on e-court and look at the booklets together - tab 22 should be 65 ter 5625, as you've identified, P316, and it should be an intercept dated 10 July 1995, report number 532, and it should indicate at the first line of text that it is a continuing -- a continuation of the conversation from report number 531.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir [sic], I understand that, but where is the time noted of 21 hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, yes. Now I understand -- now I understand, Mr. President, your question. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I was not asking Mr. Tolimir, but Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now I understand Your Honour's question. The approximate time that we've placed on the index for this is based on a corresponding intercept taken by Croatian authorities. I believe you will hear testimony, because our intercept heaven is going to continue beyond the next two weeks, you will hear testimony from Croatian intercept operators, and I believe there is a Croatian intercept. In other words, there were Croatian intercept operators who intercepted this very same conversation, and they have placed a date -- I mean, a time of 2100 hours, if I'm not mistaken, on their report. And these are two separate armies, two separate areas, both listening to the same conversation. That's what -- that's what the evidence we will proffer to Your Honours on that issue will show. So -- and if you go back and look at report number 531, which is indicated here, you'll see that that precedes the 2100-hour time, and that's why we've listed an approximate time of 2100 hours here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I believe that was produced by the OTP for the purpose of this list, but it doesn't -- that document itself, the intercept, doesn't contain any indication of the time; only the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct, Your Honour. If you look at the original ABiH intercept in the original language, it flows chronologically by the date and the report, but there's no time. It just says this is a continuation of the prior -- of the conversation at the prior report number 531. As I said, this is report number 532.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. The documents P306 through P316 will be received under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, as to the last intercept in your booklet, Witness, this is at tab 23, and this is P317.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, it should not be broadcast, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I just ask you, Witness, if you could take a moment to review this intercept again. And I want to know whether you have any independent recollection of this intercept which was taken on the 25th of July.

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Yes, this does ring a bell, sort of.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I understand if it doesn't ring any particularly loud bells 15 years after the fact, Witness. Let me ask you -- turn your attention to one remark at the end of the intercept where it's written: "During the conversation, we concluded that person X is, in fact, Milan Gvero." Do you see that? And if you do, do you have any recollection of how it was that you were able to make this conclusion that you note here at the end of your report?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Well, you see, occasionally we introduced remarks at the bottom. If there were things we were uncertain of in a certain conversation, say the identity of a person, or if we were subsequently able to identify that person, then such a remark would be made. Sometimes a person identifies himself or herself later on during the conversation. On other occasions, we were able to do that by recognising the person's voice. We had such examples with Rajko Banduka [phoen], who was at the position of secretary at the Main Staff. And at first we thought he was just a signalsman, but later on we recognised who he was. He would sometimes make remarks to the effect, Well, I'm going to put you through to Milan Gvero, or something like that. We would simply remark on that towards the end of the conversation. Of course, we made use of such identifying features in order to identify the participants.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And while we're on that topic, what other means or methods would you use to identify a speaker in a conversation, aside from, for example, the -- Mr. Banduka, the secretary you described, overtly introducing somebody by their name during the conversation?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Of course, we were able to identify certain speakers by their tone of voice, since they conversed frequently with others. At a certain point in time, we knew with certainty who some of the speakers were because of their voices. Perhaps I should add this as well: There were certain topics and a number of conversations; and in the course of the first few conversations, we were unable to a certain speaker, whereas that speaker would identify himself or herself later on and the whole group of conversations included the same topic. So by the end of that topic, of that group of conversations, we were able to pin-point the identity of a certain speaker.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So before you would write down a remark like the one we just looked at at the end of this intercept, identifying the participant as General Gvero, how certain would you have to be of that person's identity before putting it in a report?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Well, you see, if I hadn't been certain about somebody's identity, either I would not have written it down or I would have written "probably" or "likely." But if I was sure, then I would have recorded that as me being sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And as an intercept operator, sir, why was it important for you to make a distinction between, on the one hand, noting that this is, for example, probably General Gvero versus putting in the report that you have identified the speaker as General Gvero?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Because we tried very hard to do a good job, as good a job as possible. We wanted to be as correct as possible. We wanted to make -- avoid making mistakes and record mistaken identities. Even if we subsequently found out who was speaking, we would subsequently record that by way of a remark. We would note who the persons in the conversation were.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note we're approaching the break. I only have two more questions for the witness, but I can certainly pick those up after the break, to be short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it's better to -- if it's only for some minutes, you should conclude your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Then I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, let's look at P293 on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, again, it should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if you want to look at the hard copy, it's the first tab, number 1, tab number 1 in your booklet, for anybody that's using the old-school method. Do you see that there, sir? It's a report number 526, dated 9th of July.

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And was this the typical heading and format of one of your own -- that is, one of your MUP SDB intercepts, to have "CSB-SDB Tuzla" at the top of the report?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Yes, my colleague and me started our reports in this way or a similar way, according to the instruction that we had received. This is exactly how we started our reports, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at one more document. And this is P310, please. Again, not to be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, this is at tab 16 of your booklet. Please just let us know when you've had an opportunity to look at it, once you've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And this document should not be broadcast either.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you have a document that's headed "Armija Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina"?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I will not identify the location that is listed there, but do you have a report, and it includes report number 521, but with the ABiH heading at the top? Do you see that report, sir?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And for the record, the ERN is 0320-5142.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you just explain for the Trial Chamber how it is -- and if we just look at the document, we see the "CSB-SDB Tuzla" heading right above the report number 521. But at the top of this document, as a whole, it's an "armija" document, it's an army document, but with a MUP report enclosed. Can you just explain for the Trial Chamber how that happens?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. I know that we handed over our reports to the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, to the relevant department. It was only normal for us to provide the same materials that we had to the BiH Army. If we had materials, there was no reason for us to hide anything from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. That concludes my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We must have our first break now. The tapes must be rewound. And we will resume five minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I neglected to tender one final intercept in the booklet, and that is number 317.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, you know the accused, Mr. Tolimir, has the right to put questions to you. Mr. Tolimir, your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Once again, I would like to welcome everybody in the courtroom. I would like to greet the witness. I'll have a few questions for him with regard to his previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since we're speaking the same language, I would kindly ask him to wait for me to say, Thank you, and once the cursor has stopped moving on the transcript, then you start answering my question, in order to avoid overlapping.

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Court please produce P292. This is the witness's statement provided to the OTP. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the document to be produced, I'm going to put my question. Before January 2007, did anybody contact you in -- did anybody contact you with regard to your testimony before this Tribunal? Thank you. We have the first pages of the document on the screen, but let me ask you, once again: Did anybody contact you before January 2007 with regard to the testimony either here or in some other courts?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Before I provided my testimony, I was contacted maybe a month or two before. I don't know exactly. A person came to contact me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was that person from the Prosecution, and do you know that person's name? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: I believe that the person is from the Prosecution, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did they approach just you or everybody and that's why you don't know that person's name? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: I don't know the person's name. She was a lady. I don't want to make a mistake. And there were three of us during our initial conversation that I was also involved in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you asked to provide a statement, and were you told that you would be asked to testify?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Yes, we did mention our future testimonies. We were asked whether we were willing to testify before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did that person know that you had the documents that you are testifying about or did she not know?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: I don't know whether she knew or not. She just contacted us as prospective witnesses. I don't know whether she was aware of the documents or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. I apologise. Could you please tell us, before the interview that you're talking about, a month before January 2007, when you were contacted by that person, did you have these materials on you? Where were they?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: No, I didn't have those materials on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us if you know where those materials were in January 2007? Who were they with?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: The first time I saw these materials was when I came here to The Hague. They were to -- before I appeared in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell the Trial Chamber when was that? What year, if you can't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: That was in the year 2007, in the month of January. I was here for four or five days. Before I appeared in court, a couple of days before that, I had an occasion to peruse the materials.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please see the second page of the document that we now have on our screens. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: While we are looking at the second page: Did you need to seek approval from your employer in order to come and testify?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: It was a matter of courtesy for me to tell them that I was called to testify, because I had to ask for a leave of absence. And I did not encounter any problem with this regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So you just told them that you would go; you didn't have to ask their approval?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Yes, I did receive a piece of paper that I presented to them, showing where I was going, how long I would be here. And based on that piece of paper, I was relieved of my duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Once again, for the transcript, were you given consent from your employer to testify before the International Court; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, before the month of June 1995, were you a member of the Intercept Service or not?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Before July 1995, I was not a member of that service.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I interrupt you very shortly. We received the answer "Yes" in page 36, line 2. I saw the witness, that there was a sign of doubt. Could you please give the answer again? Mr. Tolimir asked you: "Were you given consent from your employer to testify before the International Court; yes or no?" Which is your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, in January 2007, did your brother also testify in that case, like he did in mine, before you?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: If we're going to talk about that, I think it would be advisable for us to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: He testified just like you did. I'm not going to ask for any names. I'm just asking you whether he testified in 2007.

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In 2005, before you joined the service, did your brother work in the State Security Service; yes or no? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: I did not understand. 2005?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You said that in June 2005, from the MUP you were transferred to the State Security and started working for the Intercept Service. Did your brother work in the State Security Service at the time?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: I believe that you're referring to 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for correcting me. During 1995, did your brother work in the State Security Service?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was your only boss your brother when you started working in the Intercept Service, or were -- did you have any other supervisors on the north facility?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: He was my immediate superior, and I'm not aware of the rest of the hierarchy of that service.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When you provided this statement in January 2007, was anybody else present in the room besides yourself and the members of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: The only other person was an interpreter, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In 2007, when you testified, were you proofed by an intercept service of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In the course of the seven days while you have been here, did you have contacts with anybody else but Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: No, I did not have any contacts with anybody else. I've not had any contacts since I arrived here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you contact your brother, because he also testified in the meantime? Did you contact him after he provided his testimony?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: To be honest, I sent him an SMS that I had arrived, and we did not discuss this case at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please look at paragraph 8 in your statement. We can now see it on the screen. It's the penultimate paragraph in the Serbian and English statements, both on page 2. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm going to quote something, and then I will have a question for you. And I quote: "We did not always transcribe the entire conversation which we had taped if portions of it were unimportant; for example, passages not of any military interest." My question: What was the purpose of intercepted conversations if you were the ones who determined the significance of those conversations, if you were the one to determine which portions were interesting and were not?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Let me tell you, this concerned a very particular situation. Conversations were intercepted, recorded, and forwarded the way they were recorded. But here reference is made to the parts in which two participants engaged for a lengthy conversation lasting for over 45 minutes. For example, they talk, I listened to them, and then in their conversations they tackle some private matters, some matters of no interest to me. However, I keep on listening, and then at one point they touch upon some matters of interest. Then I make a summary and I say, at a certain time in one of the conversation, This is what was said. This is what I mean when I say "summary." And those were usually conversations with lower-ranking foot soldiers or officers who sometimes conversed among themselves in the early hours of the night. They would normally discuss private matters. And only occasionally they would touch upon some things that concerned the front-line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you act the same if, for example, you had two participants of whom one was interesting and the other was not; for example, you were intercepting a conversation involving your commander, when your commander would be interesting and the other one would not be interesting? Would you also omit portions which were not relevant?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: No, no, never. In such situations, we never worked in that way. What is described here concerns informal conversations where nothing else is going on. One would come across a lengthy conversation which were not interesting, save for some little bits that were then summarised.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell me whether, while you were recording, did you omit what the other interlocutor said and only recorded what was said by the interlocutor that was of interest to you and your service?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: No, never. It happened very often at the beginning, and late more rarely, that we did not hear the second person, then we would put a line of dots and we would say that we could not hear the interlocutor. And sometimes the transmission was not clear. We would also record that, and later on we would try to reconstruct the conversation. What I'm saying is that we tried to follow the words of both interlocutors, as far as that was feasible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell me, in this binder containing intercepted conversations from 1 to 23 that the Prosecution just showed you a while ago, are there any conversations in which you could not hear both interlocutors?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Of course there are.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In this binder containing conversations from 1 through 23, are there any conversations where you can hear just one person and you could not hear others, whom you did not record?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: If I understood you properly, you're asking me whether there are any conversations in which you hear both interlocutors.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm asking you this: Are there any conversations -- I apologise to the interpreters. I'm asking you, again, are there conversations in this binder in which you can hear interlocutors on both sides when they talk to each other, but you can't hear the person whose message they are trying to convey?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that there were such conversations; for example, such a third person was not heard clearly. Sometimes you could hear a person talking on the phone, and then there was a person standing by the telephone whom we couldn't hear. There were such instances and such conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My following question is this: In this binder, are there conversations in which the words of one interlocutor are heard very well when they engaged in informal conversations, and when they tried to convey a message from a third person, for example, an interpreter, you couldn't hear that?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: I really can't answer your question. I don't have an impression that that happened. Sometimes it happened that the transmission was not clear enough, but it's very difficult for me to say when that happened and in what situations. It sometimes happened that you could hear the interlocutors very well, and then some time would pass during which you could not hear them well, and whether that information was important or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm asking you again. You've had the binder in your hands for seven days. I'm sure that you've had enough time to look at it. Are there any conversations there where you can hear an interpreter in Sarajevo talking to the participants from the Main Staff and you could not hear the interpreter conveying the message that they had received from a third interlocutor?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Let me first tell you that I've not been perusing these materials for seven days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just two things, Mr. President. One, the question was asked and clearly answered at least once. And the second, I was going to object that there was an assumption built into the question that was not in the record, and the witness answered it himself. But I just want to place that objection on the record about asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. Thayer. I wanted to be fair towards the witness. And before I presented to him what I wanted to prove, I wanted to be fair and then I wanted to ask him whether there were such conversations. I am asking him again, and then I will move on to proving my case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Are there any conversations in the binder where you can hear an interlocutor in the Main Staff and an interpreter and the interlocutors in the UNPROFOR Command in Sarajevo, you can hear them well until the moment when the interpreter conveys the message from such a person? Are there such conversations?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: I don't know. Let's come to that conversation and we can discuss it. From this position, I really can't tell you whether there were any such conversations or not. There were situations when you could hear the interlocutors and others, when you couldn't hear them. I can't really give you a specific answer to a very abstract question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. Before we move on to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir and Witness, please don't overlap. It's very difficult for the interpreters. Slow down a bit, and don't overlap. Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir's microphone is off.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I wanted to be as fair as possible to you in trying to jog your memory about the things you may have heard. It's not up to me to try to catch you unawares 11 years down the road. That is why I wanted to present the transcripts themselves. I'm asking you whether you remember, since you told the Prosecutor so, any conversations between the generals. And I can try to jog your memory about what you said about that particular transcript. You said as follows --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir's microphone is off.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "I recall certain conversations with UN officials, such as General Nicolai, General Janvier, and others. I hoped that those conversations would amount to something, and I still have that feeling with me." Is this what you said a moment ago during examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lines 4 through 10, page 26, for the sake of the Chamber and the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You said you remembered those things. That is why I'm asking you whether you recall any such conversations in which not everything was interpreted by the interpreter when conveying the message of one of the participants.

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: When I discussed my memory of those conversations, then I said that I could remember such conversations in which some generals participated, but I don't recall each and every line of those conversations, and this is not what I said. I said that I remember them in general. That was the gist of my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this statement of yours, which is only fair. I do not contradict what you are saying. If you can recall what those generals discussed, then you must have been able to hear either them or the interpreter. Otherwise, you would not have remembered it; correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Yes. We also could hear the interpreter, because they interpreted for the most part in such conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: That is why I'm asking you that. Are there any conversations in which you could not hear the UNPROFOR generals speak but that those comments are still contained nonetheless?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Well, yes, because the message was conveyed by the interpreter. I only noted down what I could hear. What I couldn't was replaced by dots.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll get to that. But before that, tell me, did you receive any information about whether your reports reached the final user?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: No. We sent it to the centre we were supposed to, and I have no knowledge of what followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me whether you were ever subsequently asked to review again a particular conversation in order to clarify portions which you were unable to decipher at the outset?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: At the time we were working on this, we kept going to certain conversations, because I remember a few of them even now where I could, for example, hear the word "Asandi" [phoen]. It was very quiet. And upon listening to it over and over again by a number of us, we reached the conclusion that this word actually was the bad pronunciation of the last name of Janvier. So I'm trying to illustrate this, how we went back to listen to certain parts to be sure. If a report had already gone out, I would follow it up with a note stating that in this and that report the person in question was actually General Janvier, rather than the unknown word of "Asandi" as we noted down initially.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In your chain of command, starting from your brother onwards, did you ever receive a request to revisit a certain conversation in order to try to clarify parts that were unclear?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I don't think so. As far as I recall, we did not have such feedback or additional requests for review. We would simply send it on. And whether anybody worked on it any further, that is something I don't know. We never listened to things again unless we did so at the very moment before sending anything out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us this, please. When there was a change of frequency on the equipment you used, how long did it take you to locate the participants in the particular conversation again on a different channel?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Well, we had two combinations at the time. When I say "combinations," I mean two sets of equipment that were prepared beforehand. And on one combination, we always kept the same frequency. And if there was nothing of interest, then we used the other one to search all the channels, trying to locate anything of interest. And if we were both free at the time -- at that moment, we would look for any additional frequencies together. Otherwise, there were no frequent changes in frequency. Most of it was well known.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have on the left-hand side P293 in e-court, and on the right-hand side of the screen P294.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And that's tabs 1 and 2 of the booklet, if anybody's following along in hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's very helpful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you see the left-hand side? This is a conversation you recorded at frequency 836, channel 13, at 11.10 p.m. Allegedly, the conversation was between General Tolimir and General Janvier. Can you hear any other participants in this conversation, save for General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: No. Only you can be heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you hear General Janvier's interpreter?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Probably not. Had we been able to hear him, that would have been noted down.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So this is the first example in which only one of the participants is heard. Now shift to the right-hand side. This conversation was taken at 10.30 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: This is number 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes. It is P33 -- or 533. It's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: I have it before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, see here, the first one says -- T says: "I'm listening." And P says: "Hello." Who is P?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Obviously, the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Okay. Then T says: "Yes, I'm listening." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Next, P says: "General Tolimir"?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Yes, and the three dots.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you hear here a speaker from the General Staff and General Janvier's interpreter?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Yes, but the interpretation was obviously interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Sorry, it was me, I just turned off the microphone.

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: I can see that we heard them, and then something was interrupted, and then it would go on. So obviously we couldn't make out parts of the conversation. When I say "hear" or "cannot hear," you must bear this in mind: This is not as if we were sitting in this room where we can hear each other well. The situation is different. It can be suddenly cut off.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this the second type of example as I mentioned ini which you can hear one of the participants and at the outset you can hear the UNPROFOR general's interpreter, and later on you could hear neither the interpreter nor the general? Is that one of such conversations?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: I can see here that at times we could, and then at other times we could not hear the interpreter. That's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
