utterances.text: Thank you. You could hear him only at the beginning of the conversation when they established communication and at the end when he said, "Do you have anything to say" in the penultimate line on the right-hand side? Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: I don't think so. There were a number of places here where we could hear the interpreter: "Do you have anything to say," and then: "Hold on, maybe we'll need to contact you." "Around what time should we do that?" So there were different moments when we could hear him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On the last -- in the last line on the right-hand side, does it say: "Do you have anything to say," and then followed by the question mark?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: In one of the lines, yes, it says: "Do you have anything to say?"

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does T say: "I have nothing to say. I would like to thank the general, and we'll speak later"?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Yes, this is what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does this conclude the conversation between the participants?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Well, I can see that he goes on. It says: "Wait."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is this the end of the conversation? Doesn't T say: "We'll speak later"?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Well, obviously the conversation was not finished. You can say, Bye, but then you can say, Wait, wait, there's something else that we want to ask you. So the conversation goes on in a normal fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The second part is between other participants. You can only hear the T. There is no P or J. There are no other participants, only the T.

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Are we looking at the same interview -- intercept? After the line: "Do you have anything to say," T says: "No, I would like to thank the general, and we'll speak later." Later on, it's -- something follows: "If we need to contact you, at what time should we do this?" So it goes on, if this is the conversation we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Look at the transcript on the screen: It is 0320-1097.

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: This is what I'm looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, look at it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Well, it is a bit difficult to peruse it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you see it now? Doesn't the last line say: "There's nothing to add. I'd like to thank the general, and we'll speak again"?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: On the screen, this is the last line, but in my booklet, this is not so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not trying to pre-judge anything. My next question is this: Before this conversation, did you intercept conversation 531, when -- where we have Generals Tolimir and Janvier as the participants and both are heard?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Where can I find that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: 531. There should be a tab. I'll tell you which one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'll try not to compound the confusion, but I think I know what the problem is. If we work with the booklets that we have, there is a print-out that we can all share and look at the same thing. I think what has been up-loaded into e-court is a slightly different version. You can see that the ERNs are the same, but if you look on the right-hand page, 0320-1097 is in the middle of the page, and there is a second page that I think may be confusing the issue. If we go to the second page, that's what is in our booklets. And you can see at the top of the right-hand page of the second page in our booklet "0320-1097." So I suggest that the general is not seeing the second page and may be being misled, thinking that that's the end of the conversation, when, in fact, if you turn the page, there's a second page of the conversation. We have it in our booklets. I've distributed the booklets to the accused. And it's just a matter of what's being shown on e-court at the moment. I think that's what's tripping us up. So if we -- it may help just to look at the booklet, if, for nothing else, for this exhibit. And we've got the second page up. In any event, it's in e-court there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now we have the second page of this document in B/C/S on the right side of the screen. This seems to be the same as the printed version we have in our binder.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Thayer, he just confirmed my assertion, and that is that you can only hear here the final part of the conversation, where you could hear the interpreter, but throughout the rest of the conversation you couldn't hear the principal messages that General Janvier wanted to convey to the other speaker.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so. I can only tell you that in certain places we could hear the participants, and there were others wherein we couldn't. I don't know whether this conveys General Janvier's message or not, but what we could hear is noted down.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you hear any other information forwarded by General Janvier, save for the information about when they were to speak next the next day?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Well, they say: "When can we talk to you, around what time?" So they communicated. It says: "Well, tomorrow morning, if needed at 6.00." So it was obvious that you were going to continue this conversation. I see no point in disputing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is this something General Janvier wanted to pass on, or was this the word -- the words -- the voice of the interpreter?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Yes, it was the interpreter, but he wasn't speaking of his own free will. He conveyed information from the general.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall a single thing that General Janvier conveyed to General Tolimir here?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, I can't remember everything. I couldn't hear the general. And I did not analyse this conversation in detail. I only know that this was recorded, reproduced the way we were able to hear at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since I'm running out of time --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir's microphone is off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem, whatever you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Tell me, please, is it possible, in the computer you used to reproduce these conversations, to have the following: That you printed out a single collocutor, and then later on this same collocutor five or ten lines later by mistake?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Well, I can't say anything specifically, but of course errors occur. Just the other day I found an error. It was possible to have typos, but I'm not aware of any specific situations like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This suffices. So such errors were possible; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about such particular ones, but there could have been typographical errors, although I'm not aware of any specific ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I did not ask about you about any specific errors. But if something like that happened, would it be necessary to include what both interlocutors were saying, because one answer can appear later and can be put in a place where it would be given a totally different significance? Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Well, if you can hear both interlocutors at least to a certain extent, then we made sure that the second interlocutor's words are recorded or the place was left for them. If you couldn't hear the second interlocutor, you made a note of that and you just recorded the words of the first interlocutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm happy with your answer. Now that we are reading those monologues when only one person is heard talking, is it possible that, for example, the 10th sentence in that monologue could be shifted from the penultimate place to the 10th place in that monologue?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: What can prove that that was, indeed, not the case? What can we follow the course of the conversation on?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: I don't know, but I know that when I listened to conversations, when I recorded them, I recorded them as I heard them. I don't know what constitutes good proof that things transpired the way they did or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I will leave it to the Trial Chamber whether technical problems are possible or not. We just saw technical mistakes.

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: I'm not sure that this is a technical mistake. Are you referring to the situations when only one interlocutor could be heard?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I asked you whether there were conversations in the binder where you can hear just one interlocutor in their monologues. And I proved it by pointing to the letter T.

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Yes, there were such situations where we could hear only one person and not the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please wait. Now carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, I just asked you whether it was possible for those dots or those lines, where T is speaking, could be mixed up in the computer. Is it technically possible? Could line 10 then be shifted to line 22? Is that -- such a computer error possible?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not sure that the computer could be responsible for such errors.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please now look at report 532. In your binder, it is under tab 22. Thank you. The document number is 5316, page 2.

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Are you saying "531"?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's tab 22. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I just want to make sure we're all on the -- literally on the same page. It depends on exactly which conversation General Tolimir is referring to. If he's referring to report number 531, although that is included within the report that's at tab 22, what we have at tab 22 is actually another intercept that's in that same report. So we have an English translation of number 532 under tab 22. So if we really do want to look at tab -- I mean, if we really want to look at report 531, let me see if I can find that in the booklet and get that number so that we have an English translation of report 531, and that is at tab 21, the prior tab.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Exactly. Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on. Do you want to deal with number 531? Then everybody should look into tab 21.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have 531 under 22, I'm looking at it, and I intend to put a question to the witness or a few questions with regard to the document under tab 22.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's right, but the English translation is only under tab 21, and the B/C/S version as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 5315 shown on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you referring to the 65 ter number?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, I'm talking about what was given to me by the OTP to prepare myself for the conversation with this witness, and that is in binder tab 92 [as interpreted]. The page number is, as I've already stated -- I can't see that, I can't see that. My legal adviser is going to read the Prosecutor's numbers to you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think the problem is that you mix up what is behind and what is before the number. If you take the binder, if you are looking at tab 21, it is behind -- the document is behind the number, it's the next page, and there is the translation number of this intercept, number 531 in English and the B/C/S version. Behind number 22, you will find 532 only in English, but in B/C/S you will find the intercept 531 and 532.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if I may add, Mr. President, we can see that that's an example, tab 22, of the army passing on the MUP's report up its own army chain of command. That's why it shows up again. The first one is the MUP report alone, as the MUP sent it to their centre, and then we see it show up again because the army is passing on that very same intercept to its own people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this help. Mr. Tolimir, is that clear now? In that case, you should carry on and put questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I said that it is page 22 in my binder, and you're reading from page 22. Never mind. I can put questions on any of the pages, even on the page quoted by Mr. Thayer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In the conversation that Mr. Thayer wants us to look at, can you hear the interlocutors on both sides, in the Main Staff as well as in the UNPROFOR headquarters? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Yes, occasionally you can hear the second -- the other side, and occasionally you can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can we at all hear what General Janvier says to Tolimir? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: You can see "P" standing for the interpreter, meaning that the interpreter is conveying the messages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you find a single message that the interpreter conveys that reflects either the opinion or request on the part of General Janvier?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Please bear with me just for a moment. I would like to be able to read the whole conversation. I can't tell you, without reading, off the top of the head.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: If the Trial Chamber will allow you, I don't mind you reading the entire report.

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: The first one that I've come across immediately, it says: "Very well." The general says: "Your units down there are attacking our soldiers." Then one part is inaudible. "Is that correct?" I suppose that it is important what the general says here, that his soldiers had come under attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Go on reading, and then I'll have questions for you that you will be able to answer after having read the entire document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Trial Chamber whether you know what General Janvier was saying here, what the interpreter was saying on his own behalf, what he was saying on behalf of General Janvier, and what interlocutor T was saying on his own behalf? Can you make any conclusions after 20 years?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: As I'm reading things today, I can see that the interpreter was conveying the messages from General Janvier and that you are delivering your own messages, messages on your own behalf.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So you are saying that we are exchanging messages. Thank you. Please tell me, whose messages are more numerous, whose words are more often quoted, whether Janvier's words or his interlocutor on the other side?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: I would have to count words, actually. I suppose that you spoke more, that you -- in any case, your words are better heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you say that you have made a selection of the sentences told by Janvier; in other words, whether you screened those things that could be presented to the Trial Chamber and others that could not be presented?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: If we follow that logic, we would have to omit everything, because you can see here that it says: "Our soldiers came under attack." No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for your interpretation. Can one draw a conclusion from this whether this was a dialogue or a monologue?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Well, this was a dialogue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So in terms of the contents, was that a dialogue or just -- was that just one side heard and the other interlocutor could not be heard?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: You can hear the other interlocutor who is conveying General Janvier's messages, which determines this conversation to be a dialogue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: What messages did you just mention? Could you please tell us whether you recorded this conversation?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: I remember this conversation. I remember some of the details. Whether I personally recorded it or reproduced it, I wouldn't be able to tell you. I'm not sure. I can see that my colleague signed his name here. We had a formal arrangement that one of us recorded, the other reproduced. Our desks were really close, so it wasn't really important. So even if I was mistaken and put my name first and then his name second, it would not mean a lot, because both of us were involved in the contents. I was recording; the other one was reproducing. So I'm familiar with the conversation, is what I'm trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please now tell me, after this conversation, conversation 532, was that recorded by you, interceptors from the State Security Service?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This is another conversation on page 22, where it says -- follow-up is on the conversation 531 conducted between General Janvier and the aggressor General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: I believe that it was my colleague who recorded that other conversation. What's your question, actually?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since the telegram is not signed, you can see in the binder it is not signed -- for the record, we're talking about 5316. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: I don't know. All of mine are signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I have one that is unsigned in the Prosecutor's binder, 22, under tab 22.

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: 532 report?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: 532 report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is this behind the page 22?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should look at the last page in B/C/S. Sorry, the second-last page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Who was it from the State Security who recorded that important -- or, rather, it's not important. Who is it? But was it the State Security Service?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you hear in this conversation what P is demanding or requesting from T?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: It says here: "Well, tell me, what did you mean -- what did you manage to do in the meantime?" And then your response is to the effect of what you had managed to achieve in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: How come you could hear both interlocutors on both sides of the wire?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Let me tell you. I am not an expert for this type of technology. I can't tell you how connections functioned. I was the one who intercepted the recorded conversation. I would be the one sitting at the table for 16 hours and listening in. When it comes to the technical side of the technology, maybe you should talk to somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: No, I don't want to discuss the technicalities of the job. You are a [indiscernible] professional, but my question is this: How come that you can hear two interlocutors in one part of the conversation, on the same channel, on the same frequency, and then the other part of the conversation you could hear them so well?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Let me try and explain. And I repeat, there may be somebody else better suited to explain. There are telephones which have a better receiver in their electronic combination, and you could hear an interlocutor using that kind of telephone. It's down to the technical equipment, to the telephone that the other interlocutor was using, and so on and so forth. This is something that I am kind of familiar with, but I can't give you any details. It is possible that you could hear the interlocutor on the other side if they were using a better telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that whenever the interpreters participated from Sarajevo, as well as those from the General Staff, that the mic on the Sarajevo side was always poorly heard?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: I presume that they always used the same phone, the same location, but I cannot say that with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: They had a single telephone in the UNPROFOR office, and there was another one at the General Staff. They could communicate directly. They didn't need to dial any special numbers?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Well, if you say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: What I'm asking you is this: Was it technically possible that you could always hear the speaker from the General Staff and that you were never able to hear the person on the UNPROFOR side, and only occasionally you could hear their interpreters during the informal part?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: We had your channel frequency, and when you picked up the phone in the General Staff, I could hear you very well. As for the other side, we could sometimes hear them and sometimes could not. Only later we managed to locate a duplex frequency on which we could hear the other end of the line much better. It was at a later stage. In order to hear the other end of the line, technically speaking, I'm not well versed to be able to tell you how that could have been done, but I think it had to do with the phone they used and what frequency combination they used. I don't know whether this suffices.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, it suffices for you to say that there were reliable and a less reliable conversation you are presenting. Just a moment. When conclusions are drawn about what one person is saying to another, were those conclusions always clear cut and could that include all the conversations?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Well, I cannot accept what you just said. Every conversation we recorded, we did so authentically the way we heard it. Each transcript reflects the situation of what we could really hear at the moment. This is what I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When you came to the State Security Service in 1995 to work on their surveillance, did you attend any training for those engaging in intercepts and surveillance?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Well, the training we received was to the extent that our boss told us what to do and what the frequencies and equipment were, as well as what was the point in doing that. Given that I was familiar with the equipment and had worked with radio equipment before, it wasn't very difficult to fit in. It was easy for me to work on that job.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether you attended any training, be it two, five, or ten days for any radio interceptors?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: I attended no special training, save for the training we internally organised. We also carried out research, and all was done under his supervision.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did your boss attend any training?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: I don't know. You should ask him, if you ever have a chance to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: As far as we could see, your boss was your brother, because he testified here.

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: I was there only for a short while, six or seven months. I didn't work for the service for years to know whether he had attended any training.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, he told us so. He also said that he was abroad for training. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: No, we didn't discuss that, and I don't think it would be fair for me to speak about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, he told this to the Court. He said that he attended training abroad. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: I didn't. I'm not sure he ever told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So you don't know that he attended intercept training abroad; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you attend any training abroad or did you go abroad at all during the war?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: No. I never went abroad, actually, before coming here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is it possible that a certain report in the binder we saw was taken by another service and was still logged as a report of your State Security Service?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: The reports before me are ours. I am not familiar with any other reports, and I don't know what others did. What is before me is what we did and forwarded to the centre. This is what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: During examination-in-chief, could you hear from the Prosecutor that a part of the conversation between J and T, Janvier and Tolimir, was recorded by Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: I seem to recall the Prosecutor mentioning that, but I'm not familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When the Presiding Judge asked about the time of the intercept, it had to do with that. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: I remember the Prosecutor saying so, but I don't know of anyone else recording intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, is it still recorded as your intercept?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: No, these intercepts were recorded by me. As for any others, I don't know of any services doing that, and no one ever gave me anything to sign that would have to do with that. What I signed is my conversations. Whether someone else intercepted at other locations and provided that to the Prosecutor's Office, this is something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you for your testimony. You testified fairly about what you know, and I didn't want to ask you about anything else. Thank you. This concludes my cross-examination. I would like to thank the interpreters and the effort they put in to conveying the entire conversation, since we frequently overlapped. I'm well aware of that. I would also like to thank the Presiding Judge. Witness, thank you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Thayer, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I do, just very briefly. Just a couple of very small points, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell the Trial Chamber why, in the original reports, the reports that are in your language from the MUP that we have in your booklet, why the interpreter is designated with the letter P? Can you just explain that to us, please?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: Because the first letter of the word "Prevodilac," meaning "Interpreter," is P.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, one final question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You have explained that you signed the intercepts with your first name. I see sometimes that there is another name added to your name. Without mentioning that name, could you explain why there are sometimes two names?

utterances.speaker: PW-025
utterances.text: I think there are always two names. There was an internal arrangement. We put our names there because we were not members of the service. Their employees had their code-names and numbers, whereas we put our names down. The first name was the person sitting at the desk recording, then a slash, and the second name was the transcriber's name, the person typing it into the computer and sending it. Sometimes we changed places. However, for the most part, on our team, I basically sat at the desk with the equipment and my colleague typed it in, since he was a better typist, and he was the one transmitting it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. You will be pleased to hear that this concludes your examination of today. You are now free to go back to your normal activities. The Chamber would like to thank you for your attendance here in The Hague again, and all the best for your future. Thank you very much again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We should have the second break now. I think it's a convenient time to enable this witness to leave and the next witness to come into the courtroom. Thank you. Please wait a moment so the screens should be closed, and we will rise together. We break now and resume in half an hour at 10 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I apologise for our delay. Could the next witness be brought in. First, the screens have to be closed, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Please be patient for a moment. Good afternoon again, sir. Would you please read aloud the affirmation to tell the truth which is shown on the card to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There are protective measures in place for you. Your voice and face will not be acknowledged outside the courtroom. And Mr. Thayer has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. In line with your protective measures, I'd like to show you a document.

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: Good morning -- good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a document on the computer, and it's P323. I think last time around we did this on a piece of paper and handed it to you, but we're just going to show you on the computer screen. I ask you if you can confirm whether or not you see your name on this document before you.

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Witness, do you recall providing a signed witness statement to the Office of the Prosecutor back in January of 2007?

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you read that witness statement recently in your own language?

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just to move things along a little bit: You identified two corrections to that statement, did you not?

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So may we have 318 on e-court, please. And before I get too far ahead of myself, Mr. President, the Prosecution would tender P323, the pseudonym sheet, at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Witness, do you see a copy of your witness statement in your own language before you?

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. If we could turn to page 2 in both the English and the B/C/S versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to focus on the two corrections you pointed out to me at paragraph 6 first. And, actually, in the B/C/S version, it's going to be over on page -- it's going to continue over to page 3. So just please let us know when you've read the first part of paragraph 6 on page 2 and need the page turned.

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. If we could have the next page in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, I just want to focus your attention on the last sentence in paragraph 6, and I'll just read from the English translation. What is written here is: "I do not recall receiving orders to move their antennas; I did not have the know-how." Now, you pointed out a correction to me when you re-read your statement last Monday. Can you just tell the Trial Chamber what the correction is, please?

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: Yes. The last sentence of this paragraph, paragraph 6, it says: "I don't remember receiving orders to move their antennae; I wasn't trained for that." This phrase, "their antennae," I actually meant the antennae installed by my predecessors that were to serve for our -- for the purposes of our work. It had to do with the antennae we worked with --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. So if fair so say instead of "their antennas," it should simply read "our antennas"?

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. On to the next paragraph, paragraph 7. In the middle of the paragraph, you pointed out an error in the following sentence, where it says: "We would later transcribe the conversation onto teleprinter paper, then type their handwritten transcription into a laptop, encode the transcript, and transmit it." Would you please tell the Trial Chamber what correction you made to that sentence, please?

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: The sentence reads: "We tried to be 100 per cent certain that what they wrote was correct." As a matter of fact, we tried to be 100 per cent certain that what we were writing was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Actually, thanks for your attention to detail. You found another correction that I wasn't even referring to. So what you were pointing out is in the English, it's going to be page 3 of the English translation, it says: "We wanted to be 100 per cent sure of what they were writing down." And what you're telling us is that should read: "We wanted to be 100 per cent sure of what we were writing down." Is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And let me call your attention to another sentence in paragraph 7, and in your language it's the -- I believe it's the third sentence that begins: "We would later transcribe the conversation onto teleprinter paper, then type their handwritten transcription into a laptop, encode the transcript, and transmit it." And I'll just ask you, is there a correction that needs to be made in that sentence as well or not?

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: The word "handwritten" is not necessary. It also says "type out by hand." Well, what other way there would be, other than using your hands to type something into the computer? Okay, I see now. This is the context. Then we would type out the handwritten notes, so we would take down the intercept onto teleprinter paper, just plain paper, which we could make corrections to, for the sake of precision, in case someone was able to hear anything better later on when reviewing the conversation. It happened sometimes that we would together listen to a portion of the conversation to be certain, and then we could make corrections on that piece of paper. Such a finished version would be then transmitted into the laptop, encrypted, and sent to the base.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. In the English translation, it says: "We would later transcribe the conversation onto teleprinter paper, then type their handwritten transcription into a laptop ..." My question to you is: Whose handwritten transcription would be typed into a laptop? Is it theirs, or somebody else's, or "ours," or what is it, and is there actually an error there as I've read it to you?

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: Yes, I meant to say myself and my work-mate who at that moment was typing on the laptop, entering the intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Witness, with those corrections noted, can you attest to this Trial Chamber that your witness statement that you have before you accurately reflects what you said during the interview?

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: With the changes just mentioned, the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And during that interview, were you also shown a packet of six intercepts?

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Witness, were you able to determine whether or not you participated in the interception recording, transcription, or transmission of those intercept reports?

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you arrived here again recently, did you review a packet containing those same six intercepts and make the same conclusion that you participated in taking those intercepts?

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: With Madam Usher's assistance, I would just hand up to the witness his packet of six intercepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you tendering the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Sorry, old habits die hard. The Prosecution would tender P318, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received at P318, under seal. And at that stage, I would like to mention that on page 37, line 21, it should be "P323, under seal." This is the personal information sheet. The number is just missing. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I just ask you to leaf through those six intercepts behind the tabs there and ask you if you can confirm again that you were the operator who intercepted those conversations.

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: Do I have to read through all of them?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, take as much time as you need, sir, just to ensure -- I know it's been a week since you've seen that packet. But just take as much or as little time as you need to flip through those tabs and be able to confirm whether or not those are the intercepts that you were shown during your interview in 2007.

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, first can you confirm that those are the six intercepts that you were shown during your 2007 interview?

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you confirm that you participated in taking those intercepts?

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, with respect to your 2007 witness statement, can you attest before this Trial Chamber that if you were asked the same questions today that you were asked back then in 2007, that your answers would be the same?

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I want to turn your attention, sir, to the last two tabs in your booklet. That's tabs 5 and 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: For the record, one is a 4 August 1995 intercept and the other one is an 11 August 1995 intercept. And these intercept reports identify General Miletic as being one of the participants in both of these conversations. And those are P324 and P325, for the record, tabs 5 and 6 respectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: My question to you, sir, is: Do you have any independent recollection of being involved in those particular intercepts?

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you share with the Trial Chamber what, if anything, it is about these intercepts that enables you to remember anything about them today?

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: It was their arrogance towards UNPROFOR troops and their high-ranking officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this time I would tender the six intercepts contained in the booklet, P319 through P325, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: They will be received as P319, 320, 321, 322, 324, and 325.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Forgive me. I forgot that there was a gap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: All under seal. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to read the 92 ter statement summary for the Chamber at this time. The witness was trained as a teleprinter operator and cryptographer during his mandatory JNA service. Prior to the war, he worked as a communications officer, supporting the State and Public Security Services. During the war, he worked as a cryptographer, receiving and sending encrypted and open dispatches in support of the Public Security Services. He also became a Ham Radio operator during the war as a way of helping people stay in contact with their families. From June 1995 through early 1996, he began working shifts for the State Security Services at the northern site. He had no prior intercept operator training and received instruction from his direct supervisor. He worked seven-day shifts with a colleague, though sometimes his direct supervisor was present as well. The ABiH also had personnel at the northern location who worked separately. The witness intercepted primarily high-level politicians and military personnel and became familiar with their channels and voices. At the time, he knew that Generals Miletic, Gvero, and Tolimir were top VRS commands and was familiar with their voices but did not know their functions. The witness described the procedure used when intercepting, taping, and transcribing VRS radio communications as follows: They had a receiver to which was attached a scanner that was constantly running. Once the channel was picked up, they would listen to the conversation. And if it were important, they would begin recording it with an attached UHER recorder. They would later transcribe the conversation onto teleprinter paper, then type their handwritten transcription into a laptop, encode the transcript, and transmit it. If a portion of the conversation was unclear, they would listen to it over and over together until they were sure. If they were still unsure, they would place dots, a question mark, or Xs. Because the handwritten transcriptions would often get quite marked up during this process and because the typed intercept was the most important product, the handwritten pages would be collected and burned. The witness and his colleague worked as a team and would seek each other's assistance listening to the conversations, sometimes both transcribing the same intercept, then comparing their handwritten transcripts as another way of achieving the greatest possible accuracy. The two-name designation at the end of the print-outs was supposed to indicate the interceptor first and the typer/cryptographer second. However, because they worked so closely, they both often listened to the intercept. If the conversation were urgent, they would immediately remove the tape, place it on another tape machine, and begin transcribing. On rare occasions, when his direct supervisor was present and an extremely important conversation was intercepted, his supervisor would take their handwritten transcript and the tape to the base to be transcribed there. The witness reviewed six intercept print-outs, recognised his name on them, and confirmed that he participated in intercepting them. Now, sir, I just want to ask you one follow-up question. If we could have P306 on e-court, please. And let's not broadcast that, please. And that is not in this witness's booklet. This is in the prior witness's booklet, but we'll see it on e-court shortly. And if you happen to have the prior witness's booklet, it's tab 12 of the prior witness's booklet.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, do you see an intercept report number 512 dated 8 July 1995 before you?

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And is the time 1530 hours?

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we may turn to the second page in the English, and we can stay on this page in the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And this -- again, it's not being broadcast, so I don't want to mention the name here, but do you see at the very bottom there's a reference to someone who is, and I quote: "... going to bring the rest of it. He is here with us and heading towards you." Do you see that language there, sir?

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you please explain to the Trial Chamber what that line is about, please?

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: In the cases when our supervisor visited us whenever he could, in view of the fact that he had commitments in the base, when he visited us and when he came across an interesting conversation, a very interesting conversation to be more precise, because of the urgency of the matter and in order to assist us, he would take the tape and whatever was transcribed up to then and he would drive all that to the base in his car. And that -- such a case is demonstrated in here. That's what I stated in my statement. I said that things like that could happen and, indeed, did happen. And here you have one of the things that prove it. The last sentence in this document proves that such things did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, Witness, I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thayer. Mr. Tolimir, do you have cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I do have a few questions, by your leave. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Court please produce the statement that the Prosecutor displayed just a minute ago. The document number is P318. The witness provided that statement to the OTP on the 20th and the 21st of January, 2007. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can see the first page of the statement that we will be using for the first question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please tell me, before the 20th and 21st of January, 2007, did you have any contacts with anybody with regard to the things that you're testifying about today in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did any representatives of the Tribunal speak to you before those two dates, a woman?

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: Not about the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did anybody from the OTP speak to you before the 21st?

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: I received an invitation to come here, and that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In other words, your interviews in 2007 were conducted in The Hague, or did you do it in your own place, in your territory?

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: I'm not clear what you're asking me. What interviews?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Where were you on the 20th and 21st of January, 2007, when you provided your statement to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: It was here at the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether before that anybody in Bosnia-Herzegovina or, rather, in the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina spoke to you or told you that you were supposed to testify in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: Of course, somebody had to invite me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you receive consent from any of the BiH bodies to come and testify here in The Hague? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: Only from my superior in my work-place, where I still work.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I repeat my question. Before this interview, did a certain person contact you, a person from the OTP? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: Yes, a person who invited me and who defined my date of travel, and that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In other words, you did not have any other contacts with the representatives of the Prosecution - thank you - in 2007? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: No, not about the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On the statement that we see on the screen, did you read it and sign it when you first provided it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you sign the corrections that you just mentioned during your examination-in-chief, those mistakes that you had just recently noticed?

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: Yes, I signed, but these are technical corrections, corrections of mistakes of technical nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you make those corrections during the Popovic case? And if you did, was that recorded in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: I don't understand what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In the Popovic case transcript, did you notice that the same mistakes had been made, and did you remove them?

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: No, I have removed them now here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does that mean that you stated one thing at the previous trial and now you're stating a different thing, all that with regard to your original statement?

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: No, no. These are typos or mistranslations. But when it comes to my statement, my statement was the same then as it is today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us who was present in the room in which you provided the statement which we see on e-court?

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: Who was present?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes. Do you remember who was present? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: Well, you have them all mentioned on the front page, all those who were present.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm asking you whether there was somebody else besides those who are stated on the front page of the statement.

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was nobody.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you remember or do you not remember? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: I remember it very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you had worked as a cryptographer in the State Security. Could you please explain, for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, what is the job of a cryptographer?

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: Coding and decoding of strictly-confidential documents. Is that enough?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Enough, yes. Could you please -- thank you. I apologise. Could you please explain, for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, whether you were allowed to correct anything in the documents that you were given to code or decode while you were working in the State Security Service before the war?

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: At that time, I was not the one who transcribed the tapes. I received them already completed, and they had to be checked before being dispatched.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This means that you were not supposed to correct anything in the documents that you either coded or decoded; you had to code and decode everything, even the question marks and things like that?

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: Yes, exactly, and this applied both to the procedure of dispatching such documents as well as their receipt.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. How often did your supervisor come to visit you in the northern site where you were engaged in the interception work?

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly, but that all depended on his commitments in the base. He came often. He would even spend the night, if there was a lot of activity on the channels. Sometimes he would even spend the night, as I say. He came usually during the day, he would spend an hour or two with us, and then he would go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Tolimir. Mr. Tolimir's microphone is not on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You said that -- thank you, thank you, thank you, Mr. President. Thank you. Witness, you said in your statement, on page 1 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can page 1 please be displayed on e-court, paragraph 6. Actually, it's page 2. We are looking at page 1 now, and I would like the Court to produce page 2, paragraph 6, for the benefit of the witness, to jog his memory as to what he stated. I apologise. It is not paragraph 6. Could you please turn to the following page. Thank you. Thank you. Now we can see the complete paragraph 6. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You say here in paragraph 6 that you mainly intercepted politicians and high-ranking officers. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: In any case, we found those the most interesting for us, but there were other people whom we listened in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you, in the course of 1995, intercept a conversation of anybody else but generals and politicians from Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: Our range was very broad, so we were able to intercept the conversations of common folks, but we did not find their conversations interesting. We searched for the frequencies with interesting conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In your work, did you co-operate with the BiH Army and did you set priorities, did you split priorities?

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: No, we did not split priorities between ourselves. However, if there was something interesting, in military terms, then we would send our conversation to them and vice versa. They would seed to us those things that we might have found interesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please look at paragraph 7, the penultimate sentence that you can see on this page, paragraph 7, and that sentence starts with the following words, and I quote: "Since the pages became messy and since the typed documents were the most important product, the handwritten pages would be collected and burned." Did I read your words correctly?

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is that what you did with your handwritten pages, the ones that were recorded in note-books and on loose pieces of paper? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: While we were listening to the conversations, we were liable to make mistakes. And as we listened to the same conversation over and over again, sometimes we would cross out parts of the words or the last parts of the words. Then we would hand the same conversation over to the other colleague, and the decision we jointly made was finally recorded, if it made sense for the overall context.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did it often happen that you corrected yourself, what you recorded and what you thought you heard on the first listening?

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: There was no -- there were no mistakes in the gist of the sentences, but sometimes we had to correct words, cross out the first word, and sometimes we would go back to the original solution. For example, if you just heard one part of that word and you didn't hear the rest, you would enter the word with Xs or points. If we were not sure, we would mark that with either points or Xs, indicating that we were not sure of the meaning of what we'd heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did I heard you properly? When it comes to handwritten pages, did you burn them because they were illegible by other people once you made all of your corrections on them?

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: Well, we were afraid they could end up with those who should not see them. We simply burned them because that same text, corrected, would be recorded on -- by a laptop, and that's how we sent it -- that's how we dispatched it. We did not need handwritten materials.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could such materials on laptop also be accessible to the enemy, just like the handwritten material?

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: No. Are you referring to the papers, whether those could end up in somebody else's hands, or are you referring to the laptop materials?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You said that you burned handwritten materials to prevent them from ending up in the hands of those who shouldn't have them. What about the corrected text that was recorded in the laptop; could that end up with undesirable listeners?

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could laptop signals also be intercepted as well as all the other technical means?

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: I'm not technically savvy to be able to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please answer the following question: Where and when did you burn the corrected papers? Did you burn them immediately after having entered the corrections into the laptop, or did you burn them in the course of the day at certain times?

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: There were no rules as to when those papers would be burned. It depended. We had a bag where we collected all those papers, and when that bag was full, then it would be taken out of the facility and burned there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you use shorthand? How fast did you have to type or write when you made your handwritten notes?

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: It depended on the speed of the conversations. If we understood the conversation well, we could transcribe them very quickly or we could make our handwritten notes very fast, and the same applied to the laptop inscriptions. If the conversations were not easy to understand, it took us longer. There were two of us working in one shift, so we were able to work on different segments of the work. One continued listening in, and the other was transcribing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When it comes to your handwritten pages, is it true that only you could read them, that you used some abbreviations and things like that?

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: We used abbreviations only on paper. When we typed into laptop, we used full words which could be easily understood by everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You understood me very well. What you are saying is that those papers were not neatly transcribed; it was your working material?

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: Yes, because when we transcribed from UHER, we could not hear well at every moment. We had to -- we had to replay a certain word or sentence even 10 times before we were sure what was said to be able to record that in the laptop.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please look at paragraph 7, where you made corrections during your examination-in-chief, when you were examined by the Prosecutor. Here, you're talking about the methods you used to transcribe conversations and their transcribing by laptop. Could you please tell us, how much time did you need to copy a handwritten conversation which you had intercepted, and how long did it take before you could send it to the end user?

utterances.speaker: PW-027
utterances.text: It would -- it took much more time to record the intercepted conversation on teleprinter paper. Entering a conversation into laptop was a fast procedure. I was a very skilled teleprinter operator, so typing was not a problem for me. I was a skilled typist.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us, how long did you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We are running out of time. We have reached the time of adjournment for today, and we have to break now because another trial is using this courtroom this afternoon. Could you please indicate how much time you will need for conclusion of your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will need some time to clarify facts from paragraph 7, which the witness corrected during the examination-in-chief. And once I've done that, my cross-examination will be over. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In this case, we have to adjourn now and continue the examination of this witness tomorrow. I'm sorry for that, sir, but we have to adjourn. We continue with your examination tomorrow in the afternoon at 2.15. Just to remind you, you shouldn't have contact to either party about the content of your examination. Thank you very much. We adjourn and resume tomorrow at 2.15 in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 9th day of June, 2010, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.49 p.m.,
